# Overview
## Package Description

The `bff-api` package is designed to make it easy to create backend APIs that follow the Reference Architecture. The centerpiece of the package is the `Api` (or `BFFApi` which is currently an alias) CDK construct, which generates the Infrastructure as Code necessary to create these APIs. It is designed for Reference Architecture applications, but is highly configurable and designed so that the most common needs are either automatic or enabled with simple flags.

The name is a bit misleading: though it is certainly suitable for writing backend APIs for BFFs, it is actually suitable for backend APIs for any Reference Architecture projects, including ones that have only backend components. All APIs are currently built on API gateway `RestApi` resources. Some of the features of the APIs it can build are:

* The HTTP methods and path structures supported by API Gateway, in a simple-to-specify format like `'GET /path/to/my/api/{params+}'`
* Multiple authentication types implemented by API Gateway Lambda Authorizers, including unauthenticated, standard MyPowerSchool portal session authenticator (either cookie-based or `X-Session-Ref` header based)
* Multiple API implementation mechanisms; besides the default (lambdas in TypeScript), it also supports options like direct AWS service integration, lambdas with other runtimes and languages (such as Python), and mock APIs
* Mostly-automatic CORS handling including generation of `Access-Control-Allow-Origin`, `Access-Control-Allow-Headers`, `Access-Control-Allow-Methods`, and `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials` headers.
* Automatic handling of permissions and configuration needed for backend functions to directly access the session table and call out to Unified User APIs
* Automatic basic API documentation generation, which can be supplemented with additional data models
* A number of callbacks during processing, allowing other actions such as keeps track of all the Lambdas created, "bring your own" lambdas, granting Lambdas access to external resources, conditionally vetoing endpoint creation, etc.
* X-Ray and data tracing (the latter in pre-prod only) support

## Note on "environment" and "namespace" names

Many of the configuration items of this package's constructs talk about two similar-sounding and related names:
* The "environment name" (sometimes abbreviated as `envName`), which refers to a specific deployment of the Reference Architecture application in AWS.
* The "namespace", which refers to a level of deployments of the Reference Architecture application.

For most Reference Architecture applications, there are four "namespaces":
* `dev`, which is used by the development team for development purposes
* `int`, which is used primarily by the QA team, and is the primary place where QA testing is done
* `stgus`, which is also used primarily by the QA team, it is where all the applications can be seen together in one place, and we can test for (probably unwanted) interactions between them.
* `produs`, which is the production system seen by customers.

For anything past `dev`, the "namespace" is always the same as the "environment name". In `dev`, there are two options:
* The application's main branch is always deployed directly into the fixed `dev` environment. Like the other namespace/environments, there is only one `dev`.
* Developers can do personal or "feature branch" deployments to other environment names, all of which come under the `dev` namespace. Because we are following GitOps processes, the feature branch environment names are by convention the same as the git branch name, and always are prefixed by `dev/` since they are in the `dev` namespace. So a branch name might be `dev/ESP-1234`, which deploys into the `dev/ESP-1234` environment name (which is in the `dev` namespace).

# Installation

To install, add to your project:
```
npm install @ps-refarch/bff-api
```

# Usage

## Dependencies

Typically the `Api` construct is used in concert with several other CDK constructs:
* `MFEDomain`, which does the Domain Name management. This construct is passed in as a top-level property to `Api`.
* `FeatureFlags`, which pulls in the feature flags. `Api` doesn't use these directly, but the active feature flag configuration is typically passed in as environment variables to all Lambda functions.
* `FrontEnd`, which builds an MFE's front end distribution. It is not used directly, but the `FrontEnd` can have a pass-through origin that points to the API built with the `Api` construct.

The package has the following internal `@ps-refarch` dependencies:

* [`@ps-refarch/cdk-utils`](../../cdk-utils/docs/index.html)
* `@ps-refarch/env-vars`
* [`@ps-refarch/lambda-utils`](../../lambda-utils/docs/index.html)
* [`@ps-refarch/tenants`](../../tenants/docs/index.html)
* [`@ps-refarch/uu-utils`](../../uu-utils/docs/index.html)

## Examples

Here's a basic example of a simple API that is authenticated with the session authorizer, and thus would be accessible from MFE frontend code. This also loads the feature flags defined in the project, and forwards the configuration to all Lambda functions.

```typescript
    // Load up feature flags (optional)
    const flags = new FeatureFlags(this, 'feature flags', {
      namespace,
      envName,
      defaultLambdaVars: appStackProps.lambdaVars
    });

    // Build everything that has to do with the MFE's domain.
    const domain = new MFEDomain(this, 'MFE domain', {
      envName,
      region,
      hostedZoneId: acctEnvProps.hostedZoneId,
      hostedZoneName: acctEnvProps.hostedZoneName,
      isProduction,
    });

    // Build the API itself
    const api = new Api(this, 'BFF functions', {
      // The front and back end DNS
      domain,

      // The API functions themselves.
      functions: {
        'GET /a/b': {
          // An example of a simple API that uses the default session authorizer and has
          // CORS handling
          path: 'example/src/handler',
          handler: 'handler',
          cors: true,
        }
      },

      // Base of where the function code is
      baseDir: join(__dirname, '../../functions'),

      // If it's a feature branch and/or production deployment
      isFeatureBranch,
      isProduction,

      // Stuff to set up the session authorizer
      sessionAuthorizerProps: {
        account: acctEnvProps.sessionTable?.account, // Where the session table is hosted
        envName: acctEnvProps.sharedServiceEnv, // Which shared service env, `int`/`stgus`/`produs`
        region
      },
      // Default environment variables added to every lambda. These include among other things
      // feature flag configuration.
      props: {
        environment: flags.lambdaVars,
        tracing: Tracing.ACTIVE,
        runtime: Runtime..NODEJS_22_X
      },
    });
```

## Configuration

There are a large number of configuration items available in the construct. In the table below, the configuration property name is in quasi-jq format. These are probably the most common options: see the detailed documentation for the [`Api`](./classes/Api.html) construct (and specifically the [`ApiPropsAny`](./types/ApiPropsAny.html) type) for all the options.

|Key|Type|Meaning|
|---|----|-------|
|`domain`|`MFEDomain` object|Defines the DNS names for front and backend|
|`functions`|`{[method: string]: AnyFunctionDef}`|Defines your backend functions. The `method` is a string in a format like `'GET /path/to/api'` and can include path parameters using `{param}` or `{param+}`.|
|`functions.{method}.path`|string|Path to the Lambda source code, appended to `baseDir`|
|`functions.{method}.handler`|string|Function name within the source code file.|
|`functions.{method}.cors`|boolean|True if automatic CORS handling should be done.|
|`functions.{method}.unauthenticated`|boolean|True if function should be unauthenticated. Otherwise, it will be protected by the construct's Lambda authorizer, which is usually the session authorizer (see below), but can also be a Unified User-style authenticator.|
|`baseDir`|string|Base directory for the backend function code. The `path` property of each method is relative to here.|
|`isFeatureBranch`|boolean (default `false`)|True if a feature branch deployment. This is generally true if the "environment name" is not equal to the "namespace" name (see above).|
|`isProduction`|boolean (default `false`)|True if it's a production deploymnent. This usually has to be flagged in the configuration.|
|`sessionAuthorizerProps`|object|Properties needed by session authorizer. If this property is included, this tells the `Api` construct that you want the session authorizer to be used.|
|`sessionAuthorizerProps.account`|string|The AWS account id of the session table. Normally this is `246597006913` for preprod and `688739388178` for production.|
|`sessionAuthorizerProps.envName`|string|The shared services environment name. Normally the `dev` and `int` namespaces will use `int`, `stgus`->`stgus`, and `produs`->`produs`|
|`sessionAuthorizerProps.region`|string|The region where the session table is. Should be the same as where the `Api` is being deployed to.|
|`props`|`NodejsFunctionProps` object|Set of default properties passed to every Lambda construct.|

## Authorization and Authentication

If your API uses the MyPowerSchool portal session authenticator (see `sessionAuthorizerProps` above), your code will receive the following data through Lambda context variables:

- `id_token` — A JWT for the Unified User account
- `district_uid` — A UUID for the district the user is in
- `district_products` — The same data you'd get if you called the `/district/XYZ/products` endpoint

# Other key features

## CORS handling
One of the more annoying aspects of writing APIs is CORS handling. There are various problems:

* There are multiple situations that need to be handled, but only some of them are usually considered by developers
* The browser outputs many different error messages for CORS violations, and these are quite detailed, but unfortunately sound a lot alike. It's easy to see one and assume the browser is talking about something else.
* An additional issue is that API Gateway has multiple ways of handling these different situations, depending on what kind of integration is used. The most common one (Lambda Proxy) unfortunately has to be handled differently from all the others.

As noted above, the `BFFApi` tried to make CORS handling almost automatic, assuming that you configure it properly through the construct's properties. In CORS handling, there are three general types of situations that need to be handled:

1. CORS headers on the preflight OPTIONS request, which the browser sends in certain not-easily-understood circumstances
2. CORS headers on the API request itself
3. CORS headers on error responses where the API Gateway is returning the error directly without ever invoking the Lambda. (Error responses where the Lambda is called fall under situation 2.)

`BFFApi` handles all three situations for AWS directly integrations and situations 1 and 3 for the common Lambda Proxy integrations. For Lambda Proxy situation 2, you are responsible for returning your own CORS headers. (NOTE: The QuickStart application includes sample Lambdas which use the `@middy/http-cors` package, which we believe is the best way to handle situation 2 in your own lambdas. Using this package, along with some environment variables `BFFApi` construct passes the Lambda, will make even situation 2 semi-automatic.)

## WAF rules on API docs

Originally, API docs were freely available on the internet. However, recent changes have led us to want to put the API docs behind the VPN. Thus, now by default, API docs are created with WAF rules in place that limit access to being behind the VPN. It makes use of the `APIDocsWAF` construct of the `cdk-utils` package. You can override this, but only in production.

# Contributing / Development

This repo uses `yarn` as the build tool, and `lerna` to manage the packages. To get started, run:

## Initialize and Build

```bash
  yarn
  yarn run build:all
```

## Linting
```bash
    yarn run lint:all
```

## Linting only this package
```bash
    npx lerna run lint:fix --scope=@ps-refarch/bff-api
```

## Unit Tests
```bash
    yarn run test:unit:all
```

## Unit Tests only this package
```bash
    npx lerna run test:unit --scope=@ps-refarch/bff-api
```

## Unit Tests only one file in this package
```bash
    npx lerna run test:unit --scope=@ps-refarch/bff-api -- --testPathPattern=session-authorizer.test.ts
```
